questions.q: For a Hadamard circuit run 1024 shots returning 480 counts of '0' (expected p0=0.5), what is the computed z-score?
Using that same z-score of -2.0 (480/1024 result), what is the test verdict at 95% confidence (|z|<1.96) versus 99% confidence (|z|<2.58)?
options: It fails at 95% confidence but passes at 99% confidence
It passes at both confidence levels
It fails at both confidence levels
It passes at 95% but fails at 99%
questions.explain: |z|=2.0 exceeds the 1.96 threshold for 95% confidence (fails) but is below the 2.58 threshold for 99% confidence (passes) -- the same data gives different verdicts depending on which confidence level was committed to in advance, which is why the lesson insists the threshold must be stated explicitly.

questions.q: For the same circuit returning 540 counts of '0' out of 1024 shots instead, what is the resulting z-score, and does it pass at 95% confidence?
questions.explain: phat = 540/1024 = 0.52734375, z = (0.52734375-0.5)/0.015625 = 1.75, which is below the 1.96 threshold for 95% confidence, so this result passes -- well within normal sampling variance for a fair coin at this shot count.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend a chi-square test instead of a z-test for a Bell state's measurement outcomes?
options: Chi-square tests are always more accurate than z-tests
A Bell state has more than two possible outcome categories (00 and 11 both expected, 01/10 expected near zero), which a binary z-test for a single proportion can't directly handle
Z-tests cannot be computed for quantum circuits at all
Chi-square tests require fewer shots than z-tests
questions.explain: The z-test as presented handles a single binary proportion. A Bell state's outcome space has multiple categories to compare simultaneously against expected counts, which is exactly what a chi-square test is built for.

questions.q: How does increasing the shot count from 1024 to 4096 (4x) affect the standard error, and what does that imply for test tolerance?
options: SE roughly doubles, making the test less sensitive to bias
SE is unchanged; shot count doesn't affect standard error
SE shrinks by roughly half (since SE scales as 1/sqrt(n)), tightening the tolerance and making the test more sensitive to a given bias
SE shrinks by a factor of 4, matching the shot increase exactly
questions.explain: Standard error scales as 1/sqrt(n). Quadrupling shots (4x) shrinks SE by sqrt(4)=2, i.e. roughly half -- tightening the detectable tolerance window, which is why the lesson ties shot-count choice directly to how sensitive a test needs to be.
